podcast.body: Roy Brown wrote this song, confident it would resonate with wider audiences due to its consistent success in his own live shows. He initially offered it to Wynonie Harris, who declined. After relocating to New Orleans, Brown presented it to Cecil Gant, who, deeply impressed, made a 2:30 AM call to his record company head, securing Brown a recording deal. This original version became a minor hit, peaking at number 13 on the R&B chart and later re-entering at number 11. "In particular, one called Good Rock in Tonight, he thought might be popular with other audiences, since it always went down so well in his own shows."

podcast.body: Roy Brown's original recording of "Good Rockin' Tonight" is characterized by holding the first chord and repeating the same riff for the majority of the verse and chorus. Its chord changes are closer to passing chords, resulting in a "one chord feel" that emphasizes groove over complex harmonic progression, diverging from a conventional 12-bar blues structure. "Roy Brown's original, on the other hand, just holds the first chord and keeps playing the same riff for almost the entire verse and chorus."

podcast.body: Roy Brown, a Black blues singer from Louisiana, released this hit song in 1947. Along with Wynonie Harris's version, this track helped move the notion of "rockin'" as a musical concept deeper into the public consciousness. "Some will point to a 1947 song by Roy Brown, a black blues singer from Louisiana, what I hit with a song called Good Rockin Tonight."
